# Unit 3 week 3 — Teacher answers
A: linear 101 => index0/1 probe; 117 => index4/5 probes; 999 => None/7 probes. Use result is not None. Linear returns first duplicate occurrence.
B: 117 probes (low,high,mid,value) (0,6,3,112), (4,6,5,123), (4,4,4,117), return4. For119 the third probe sets low5 with high4, then None. Sortedness makes discarded regions impossible locations. <= includes the final candidate; +/-1 excludes the tested item. Unsorted [3,1,2], target3 returns None for binary and0 for linear, illustrating invalid input rather than valid-input correctness.
C: [] => None; [5]/5=>0, [5]/4=>None. First index must be accepted. For [2,2,2], linear0 and this binary1 are both contract-correct. Input remains unchanged. Compare actual results against the stated duplicate policy.
D: absent target n yields linear 8,16,32,1024 probes; binary 4,5,6,11. Worst-case time O(n)/O(log n); iterative extra space O(1)/O(1); best-case O(1) for each. A probe can include two comparisons. Sorting or verifying order has a separate cost; sorted indexes are not original indexes. Short one-off unsorted lookup generally favours linear; repeated sorted-data searches favour binary, subject to requirements. No official task weighting assigned.
